title: Python scripts for automation
intro: Day 7 left you with Bash scripts that fail loudly, and a rule to switch to Python once a script grows. This part is that switch. Day 15 writes scripts from the standard library alone and runs them with uv. Day 16 calls the GitHub API and AWS, tests both without a network, and installs the result as commands. Every script lives in labs/python-ops, and its 30 tests run offline in about ten seconds.

lessons.title: Python for ops scripts: files, JSON, arguments and exit codes
lessons.goal: By the end you can write a Python script that reads logs, takes arguments and environment variables, reports on stdout and stderr, and returns exit codes that CI can act on, and you can run it with uv.

guess.q: Your Python script calls `subprocess.run(["git", "pull"])` and git fails with a merge conflict. What does your script do next?
options: Python raises an exception and the script stops
It carries on to the next line as if git had worked
Python prints git's error and exits with code 1
It waits until someone fixes the conflict
guess.why: `run()` only records git's exit code in the result it returns. Unless you pass `check=True` or look at `returncode`, the script carries on, like bash without `set -e`.

sections.h: When a Bash script should become Python
sections.body:
Day 7 ended with a rule of thumb: once a script needs real data structures or grows past about a hundred lines, write it in Python. Bash is very good at starting programs and wiring their output together. It gets painful as soon as you need to keep data around and make decisions about it.

Move to Python when a script needs any of these:

- Data you look things up in, such as counts per path. The bash 3.2 on your Mac has no associative arrays at all.
- JSON or an HTTP API. One `jq` call is fine. Five of them glued together with `$(...)` are a program in disguise.
- Different handling for different errors: a missing file, a timeout, a 404.
- Tests. pytest (Day 16) is far easier than testing a shell script.
- The same behaviour on macOS and Linux. `sed -i` and `date -d` differ between the two; Python's `re` and `datetime` do not.

Keep Bash for short glue: a five-line CI step, a `RUN` line in a Dockerfile, or `healthcheck.sh` from Day 7. Keep the Day 7 habits too. A Python script also needs a clear exit code, messages on stderr and a loud failure, and most of today is about doing that well.

Python is already installed on GitHub's Ubuntu runners and on Ubuntu and Amazon Linux servers. Its standard library covers files, JSON, CSV, regular expressions, time zones and running other programs, and today's scripts use nothing else. Day 16 adds the two outside packages most ops scripts need: requests and boto3.

sections.h: Python versions, environments and one-file scripts with uv
sections.body:
On Day 2 you set up hello-devops the classic way: Homebrew's Python, `python3 -m venv .venv`, `source .venv/bin/activate`, then `pip install -r requirements-dev.txt`. That still works, and hello-devops keeps it, because its Dockerfile and its CI (Day 25) use pip.

For new tools this course uses uv, one program from Astral, the company that also makes ruff. It does the jobs of Homebrew's Python, venv and pip, and a few more:

- `uv python install 3.14` downloads a Python version, so you stop depending on what Homebrew has.
- `uv init` starts a project with a `pyproject.toml`, the standard file for a project's name, Python version and dependencies.
- `uv add requests` adds a dependency and writes the exact version of every package to `uv.lock`. Commit that file, so CI and teammates get the versions you tested.
- `uv run <command>` first makes `.venv` match the lock file, then starts the command with `.venv/bin` at the front of its PATH (Day 7). That is most of what `activate` does, so you never activate anything.
- `uvx ruff check` runs a tool in a throwaway environment.

A **virtual environment** (Day 2) is still underneath: uv creates the same kind of `.venv` folder that `python3 -m venv` makes. You just stop managing it by hand.

A single script does not even need a project. PEP 723 (a Python Enhancement Proposal, one of the documents that set Python's standards) defines inline script metadata: a comment block at the top of the file. It names the Python version and the packages the script needs. The command `uv init --script check.py --python 3.14` creates the block, and `uv add --script check.py requests` adds a package to it. Then `uv run check.py` builds a cached environment with those packages and runs the script.

The lab's `scripts/logsum.py` has such a block with an empty package list. Inside a project, a script with a block ignores the project and uses only its own list. With the shebang `#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script` and `chmod +x`, you can also start it as `./logsum.py`. The `-S` makes `env` split `uv run --script` into three words; without it, `env` looks for one program with that whole name. Read a script from the internet before you `uv run` it, because uv installs whatever its block asks for.

The lab pins Python 3.14, the version in the course's Docker images and CI, in `.python-version`.

sections.h: The skeleton every ops script shares
sections.body:
Open `scripts/logsum.py` in the Files section. Every script in the lab has the same shape, top to bottom:

1. The shebang and the PEP 723 block.
2. A docstring with examples and the exit codes. It is the first thing a tired person reads.
3. Imports, then constants such as the regex for one log line.
4. Small functions that each do one job and return data. `parse_access` never prints.
5. `main(argv=None) -> int`, which reads the arguments, calls the functions, prints, and returns an exit code.
6. `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())` as the last line.

That last line runs `main` only when you start the file as a program. Python sets `__name__` to `"__main__"` in the file you ran, and to the module's name, `"logsum"`, in a file that is imported. So when a test imports the file, nothing runs. With `argv=None`, argparse reads the real command line from `sys.argv`. A test passes its own list instead, `main(["access", "x.log"])`, and checks the number it gets back, which is what Day 16 does.

`argparse` turns `sys.argv` into named values and writes `--help` for you. The summarizer uses four of its features:

- Positional arguments (`file`) and options (`--top 5`), each with a `type` that converts the text and rejects bad values.
- `choices=["text", "json"]`, so `--format xml` fails at once.
- Subcommands, like git's: `logsum access FILE` and `logsum app FILE` share their common options through a parent parser.
- Defaults from the environment: `default=os.environ.get("LOGSUM_MAX_ERROR_RATE", "1.0")`. Because argparse uses a default only when the flag is missing, a flag beats the variable, and the variable beats the built-in `1.0`.

On a bad argument, argparse prints the usage line and exits with 2, the same "you called me wrong" code that `healthcheck.sh` used on Day 7. Read settings with `os.environ.get("NAME", default)`. Plain `os.environ["NAME"]` raises `KeyError` when the variable is missing, which is right only for a setting the script cannot run without.

sections.h: Log lines into numbers: pathlib, re and Counter
sections.body:
`pathlib.Path` is how current Python handles files. `Path.home() / "code" / "linux-lab"` joins the parts with `/` on any OS. `path.read_text()`, `path.exists()` and `path.glob("*.log")` replace most uses of `open`, `os.path` and `ls`.

A regular expression (Day 4) with named groups turns one access log line into a dictionary. You name a group with `(?P<name>...)`. Write the pattern as a raw string, `r"..."`, so Python leaves its backslashes alone. In a normal string, `"\b"` becomes a backspace character instead of the regex word boundary. Try the pattern on one line in the REPL before you trust it on 238 lines.

`collections.Counter` is a dictionary made for counting. A missing key reads as 0, so `paths[path] += 1` works the first time a path appears, where a plain dict would raise `KeyError`. And `paths.most_common(5)` returns the top five. With it, one pass over the file collects everything at once: requests per path, per status class and per server error.

How does that compare with Day 5? The pipeline `awk '$9 >= 500 {print $9, $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` prints the same three lines as the summarizer, starting with `6 500 /api/checkout`. For one question, awk is shorter and much faster. The Python version pays off once you want several answers from one pass, a time window, JSON output, a limit and tests.

It also counts more honestly, because it strips the query string before counting a path. The worked example shows how far apart the two top lists end up.

For big files, loop over the open file with `for line in f:` instead of reading it all with `read_text()`. The file object hands you one line at a time, so memory stays flat, as the Go deeper section measures.

sections.h: Dates, JSON and CSV without surprises
sections.body:
Time zones are where ops scripts go quietly wrong. A Python `datetime` is either naive, with no time zone, or **aware**, with one. Comparing a naive one with an aware one raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, which is at least loud. The quiet bug is two naive values from different zones. Say you drop the `+0000` while parsing a UTC log time, then compare it with `datetime.now()`, which is your Mac's local time. Every answer is off by your offset from UTC, and nothing complains.

Three habits prevent it:

- Parse the zone the log gives you. `%z` in `strptime(text, "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z")` reads the `+0000`. `datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-30T09:00:01Z")` understands the `Z` since Python 3.11.
- Ask for the current time as `datetime.now(UTC)`. `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive value and has been deprecated since Python 3.12.
- Convert only for display. `when.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin"))` turned 09:00:08 UTC into 10:00:08+01:00. The summarizer's `--tz` option does that.

JSON is the format for other programs. `json.dumps(report, indent=2)` writes it, and `json.loads(text)` reads it. For JSON Lines, such as `events.jsonl` from Day 5, call `json.loads` once per line. When a script prints JSON, print nothing else to stdout, so `| jq` keeps working.

CSV is for people with spreadsheets. Use the `csv` module instead of `",".join(...)`, because it quotes values that contain commas. Open the file with `newline=""`, as the `csv` docs ask, or an extra `\r` ends up in each line on Windows.

sections.h: Exit codes, stderr and errors that say what to do
sections.body:
CI, systemd (Day 6), cron (the Unix scheduler for timed jobs) and Kubernetes exec probes (Day 43) decide success or failure from the exit code alone. A Python script ends with a code in one of three ways:

- `sys.exit(main())` turns the number `main` returns into the exit code.
- An uncaught exception prints a traceback and exits with 1.
- argparse exits with 2 on bad arguments.

So the lab uses one contract in every script: 0 means all good, 1 means the check found a problem, and 2 means the script could not do its job. A caller can then tell "the error rate is too high" apart from "the log file is missing".

Output goes to two places. The report goes to stdout, the only stream a pipe (Day 5) passes on. Everything for people, such as warnings, progress and the reason for a failure, goes to stderr. The `logging` module sends messages there after `logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, ...)`. Each message has a level, from DEBUG up to ERROR, and messages below the level you set are dropped. The summarizer sets INFO, and `-v` lowers it to DEBUG. Pass values as arguments, `log.warning("line %d skipped", number)`, so the text is only built when the message is shown.

Catch the errors you expect, by name, and turn each into one clear line. In the summarizer, `except FileNotFoundError` becomes `logsum: ERROR no such file: nope.log` and exit code 2. Let every other exception crash with its traceback, since a traceback is the quickest way to debug something you did not expect. And never log a token or a password, not even at DEBUG.

sections.h: Running other programs safely with subprocess
sections.body:
Sooner or later a script calls `git`, `kubectl` or `terraform`. `subprocess.run` starts the program and waits for it. Give it four things every time:

- A list of arguments, `["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"]`, which Python hands straight to the program, so no shell ever reads them.
- `check=True`, so a non-zero exit raises `CalledProcessError` instead of passing silently.
- `capture_output=True, text=True`, to get stdout and stderr back as strings.
- `timeout=30`, so a hung command raises `TimeoutExpired` instead of hanging your script.

In `/tmp`, `subprocess.run(["git", "log", "-1"], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)` raised `CalledProcessError(128, ['git', 'log', '-1'])`, and `err.stderr` held `fatal: not a git repository`. That message is exactly what to log before you exit with 2.

`shell=True` with outside input is how scripts get hijacked. With it, Python passes one string to `/bin/sh`, and the shell reads a `;` inside it as the start of a second command. With `name = "x; echo pwned"`, the call `subprocess.run(f"ls {name}", shell=True)` printed `pwned`. The list form passed the whole string to `ls` as one argument, and `ls` answered `cannot access 'x; echo pwned'`.

Environment variables flow down to the child, as on Day 7. To add one, copy the current environment: `env={**os.environ, "KUBECONFIG": path}`. Passing `env={"KUBECONFIG": path}` alone gives the child no `PATH` and no `HOME` at all.

lessons.analogy: A script reports back like a parcel delivery. The tracking status (delivered, failed, unknown address) is the exit code: it is what the depot's systems act on. The note on your door is stderr, written for a person. The parcel itself is stdout, the thing you actually wanted. Unlike a parcel, a script can hand over half its output and still fail, so a caller checks the exit code before trusting what arrived.

code.title: scripts/logsum.py (in labs/python-ops)
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = []
# ///
"""logsum.py: summarize the Part 1 sample logs (labs/linux, copied to ~/code/linux-lab).

Examples:
  uv run scripts/logsum.py access ~/code/linux-lab/access.log
  uv run scripts/logsum.py access ~/code/linux-lab/access.log --max-error-rate 5
  uv run scripts/logsum.py app ~/code/linux-lab/app.log --format json

Exit codes: 0 all good, 1 over a limit you set, 2 bad usage or unreadable file.
"""

import argparse
import csv
import json
import logging
import os
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo, ZoneInfoNotFoundError

log = logging.getLogger("logsum")

# One line of the nginx "combined" format, for example:
# 203.0.113.7 - - [30/Oct/2026:09:00:08 +0000] "GET /api/cart HTTP/1.1" 200 4642 "-" "curl/8.5.0"
ACCESS_LINE = re.compile(
    r"(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] "
    r'"(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+) [^"]*" '
    r"(?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\d+|-)"
)

# One line of app.log, for example:
# 2026-10-30T09:04:30Z ERROR checkout-api req=8e9f0a database connection refused: orders-db:5432
APP_LINE = re.compile(
    r"(?P<time>\S+) (?P<level>[A-Z]+)\s+(?P<service>\S+) req=(?P<req>\S+) (?P<msg>.*)"
)


@dataclass
class AccessStats:
    requests: int = 0
    skipped: int = 0
    first: datetime | None = None
    last: datetime | None = None
    paths: Counter = field(default_factory=Counter)
    classes: Counter = field(default_factory=Counter)
    server_errors: Counter = field(default_factory=Counter)

    @property
    def error_rate(self) -> float:
        """Server errors (5xx) as a percentage of all requests."""
        if self.requests == 0:
            return 0.0
        return 100 * self.classes["5xx"] / self.requests


def parse_access(lines) -> AccessStats:
    stats = AccessStats()
    for number, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        match = ACCESS_LINE.match(line)
        if not match:
            # A bad line should not stop a 3 a.m. report, but it must be visible.
            stats.skipped += 1
            log.warning("line %d does not look like an access log line, skipped", number)
            continue
        stats.requests += 1
        # %z reads the "+0000" part, so `when` knows its time zone.
        when = datetime.strptime(match["time"], "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z")
        stats.first = when if stats.first is None else min(stats.first, when)
        stats.last = when if stats.last is None else max(stats.last, when)
        path = match["path"].split("?", 1)[0]  # /api/products?page=3 counts as /api/products
        status = int(match["status"])
        stats.paths[path] += 1
        stats.classes[f"{status // 100}xx"] += 1
        if status >= 500:
            stats.server_errors[f"{status} {path}"] += 1
    return stats


def parse_app(lines) -> dict:
    levels: Counter = Counter()
    errors: Counter = Counter()
    times = []
    continued = 0
    for number, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        if line[:1].isspace():
            continued += 1  # a stack trace line that belongs to the line above
            continue
        match = APP_LINE.match(line)
        if not match:
            log.warning("line %d does not look like an app log line, skipped", number)
            continue
        levels[match["level"]] += 1
        times.append(datetime.fromisoformat(match["time"]))  # "Z" works since Python 3.11
        if match["level"] == "ERROR":
            errors[match["msg"]] += 1
    return {"levels": levels, "errors": errors, "times": times, "continued": continued}


def read_lines(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    # errors="replace": one broken byte must not crash the whole report.
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines()


def show_time(when: datetime | None, zone: ZoneInfo) -> str:
    return when.astimezone(zone).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z") if when else "-"


def write_csv(path: Path, stats: AccessStats) -> None:
    errors_by_path: Counter = Counter()
    for key, count in stats.server_errors.items():
        errors_by_path[key.split(" ", 1)[1]] += count
    with path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(["path", "requests", "server_errors"])
        for p, count in stats.paths.most_common():
            writer.writerow([p, count, errors_by_path[p]])
    log.info("wrote %d rows to %s", len(stats.paths), path)


def run_access(args) -> int:
    stats = parse_access(read_lines(args.file))
    ok = stats.error_rate <= args.max_error_rate
    if args.csv:
        write_csv(args.csv, stats)
    if args.format == "json":
        report = {
            "file": args.file.name,
            "requests": stats.requests,
            "skipped": stats.skipped,
            "first": stats.first.isoformat() if stats.first else None,
            "last": stats.last.isoformat() if stats.last else None,
            "status_classes": dict(sorted(stats.classes.items())),
            "error_rate": round(stats.error_rate, 2),
            "max_error_rate": args.max_error_rate,
            "ok": ok,
            "top_paths": stats.paths.most_common(args.top),
            "server_errors": stats.server_errors.most_common(),
        }
        print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    else:
        zone = args.tz
        print(f"{args.file.name}: {stats.requests} requests, {stats.skipped} skipped")
        print(f"from {show_time(stats.first, zone)} to {show_time(stats.last, zone)}")
        classes = ", ".join(f"{k} {v}" for k, v in sorted(stats.classes.items()))
        print(f"status: {classes}")
        print(f"error rate (5xx): {stats.error_rate:.1f}% (limit {args.max_error_rate:.1f}%)")
        print(f"\ntop {args.top} paths:")
        for p, count in stats.paths.most_common(args.top):
            print(f"{count:7}  {p}")
        print("\nserver errors:")
        for key, count in stats.server_errors.most_common():
            print(f"{count:7}  {key}")
    if not ok:
        log.error(
            "error rate %.1f%% is above the limit of %.1f%%", stats.error_rate, args.max_error_rate
        )
        return 1
    return 0


def run_app(args) -> int:
    result = parse_app(read_lines(args.file))
    levels, errors, times = result["levels"], result["errors"], result["times"]
    if args.format == "json":
        report = {
            "file": args.file.name,
            "levels": dict(levels),
            "first": min(times).isoformat() if times else None,
            "last": max(times).isoformat() if times else None,
            "stack_trace_lines": result["continued"],
            "top_errors": errors.most_common(args.top),
        }
        print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    else:
        zone = args.tz
        print(f"{args.file.name}: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v}" for k, v in levels.most_common()))
        if times:
            print(f"from {show_time(min(times), zone)} to {show_time(max(times), zone)}")
        print(f"\ntop {args.top} errors:")
        for msg, count in errors.most_common(args.top):
            print(f"{count:7}  {msg}")
    if args.max_errors is not None and levels["ERROR"] > args.max_errors:
        log.error("%d ERROR lines, the limit is %d", levels["ERROR"], args.max_errors)
        return 1
    return 0


def zone(name: str) -> ZoneInfo:
    """argparse type: turn 'Europe/Berlin' into a time zone, or fail with a clear message."""
    try:
        return ZoneInfo(name)
    except (ZoneInfoNotFoundError, ValueError):
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"unknown time zone {name!r}") from None


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="logsum", description="Summarize the Part 1 sample logs.")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", help="also print debug messages")
    # Settings shared by both subcommands.
    common = argparse.ArgumentParser(add_help=False)
    common.add_argument("file", type=Path, help="the log file to read")
    common.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5, metavar="N", help="rows to show (default 5)")
    common.add_argument(
        "--format", choices=["text", "json"], default="text", help="text for people, json for jq"
    )
    common.add_argument(
        "--tz",
        type=zone,
        default="UTC",
        metavar="ZONE",
        help="show times in this zone (default UTC)",
    )

    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    access = sub.add_parser("access", parents=[common], help="nginx access log")
    access.add_argument(
        "--max-error-rate",
        type=float,
        metavar="PCT",
        # A flag beats the environment variable, which beats the default.
        default=float(os.environ.get("LOGSUM_MAX_ERROR_RATE", "1.0")),
        help="fail when more than this percent of requests are 5xx (default 1.0)",
    )
    access.add_argument(
        "--csv", type=Path, metavar="FILE", help="also write per-path counts to this CSV file"
    )
    access.set_defaults(handler=run_access)

    app = sub.add_parser("app", parents=[common], help="app log with levels")
    app.add_argument(
        "--max-errors", type=int, metavar="N", help="fail when there are more ERROR lines than N"
    )
    app.set_defaults(handler=run_app)
    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    # Log messages go to stderr, so stdout stays clean for the report (and for jq).
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.INFO,
        format="logsum: %(levelname)s %(message)s",
        stream=sys.stderr,
        force=True,
    )
    try:
        return args.handler(args)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        log.error("no such file: %s", args.file)
        return 2
    except PermissionError:
        log.error("no permission to read %s", args.file)
        return 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

task.title: A URL health checker in Python
steps: Make a folder `~/code/ops-scripts`, then run `uv init --script healthcheck.py --python 3.14` in it.
Create `urls.txt` with one URL per line: the `/healthz` and `/readyz` URLs of hello-devops on port 8000, plus `http://localhost:9998/`. Your script skips blank lines and lines that start with `#`.
Use argparse for the file name and a `--timeout` option. Its default comes from a `HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT` environment variable, or 5 seconds.
For each URL, call `urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=...)` from the standard library and print one line on stdout: OK or FAIL, the URL, and a short reason.
Catch the failures by name and give each its own reason: an HTTP error status, no connection, and a timeout.
Exit with 0 when every URL is fine, 1 when any failed, and 2 for a missing file. Send the summary line to stderr with logging.
Start hello-devops (`python app.py` in its venv from Day 2) and run your checker. Then stop the app and run it again. Check `echo $?` each time.
Run `nc -l 9998` in another terminal, so that URL accepts the connection and never answers. Run the checker with `--timeout 2` and time it.
Run `uvx ruff check healthcheck.py`, fix what it reports, and compare your script with `scripts/healthcheck.py` in the lab.
hints: `urlopen` raises `urllib.error.HTTPError` for 4xx and 5xx answers. It is a subclass of `URLError`, so put its `except` first.
A refused connection arrives as `URLError`; look at `err.reason`. A timeout can arrive as `TimeoutError` or inside a `URLError`.
Only allow `http` and `https` URLs: `urlopen` would also open `file:///etc/passwd`.
task.done_when: You are done when your checker prints one line per URL, exits 0 with hello-devops running and 1 with it stopped, and gives up on the `nc` URL after your timeout.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how a script should report its result to CI and to a person. Mention stdout, stderr and exit codes, and say why a broad `except` is dangerous.
explain_back.answer: CI only reads the exit code, so the script returns 0 when all is well, 1 when the check found a problem, and 2 when it could not run. The report or JSON goes to stdout, where another program can read it cleanly. Messages for people, such as warnings and the reason for a failure, go to stderr through logging. A broad `except Exception: pass` hides failures and lets the script exit 0, so CI goes green even though nothing worked.

options: Exit code 0, because Python itself ran
Exit code 2, the code for usage errors
Exit code 1, with a traceback on stderr
No exit code until the job is killed
check.why: An uncaught exception prints a traceback to stderr and ends Python with exit code 1.

options: Python raises a TypeError about naive and aware datetimes
Python converts both to UTC and compares them correctly
The comparison always returns False
Python assumes the log time is local time
check.why: `datetime.now()` is naive and the parsed value is aware, and Python refuses to compare the two; use `datetime.now(UTC)`.

check.q: A script must run `kubectl get pods -n NAME`, where NAME comes from a command-line argument. Which call is safe?
options: `subprocess.run(f"kubectl get pods -n {name}", shell=True)`
`os.system("kubectl get pods -n " + name)`
`subprocess.run("kubectl get pods -n " + name, shell=True, check=True)`
`subprocess.run(["kubectl", "get", "pods", "-n", name], check=True, timeout=30)`
check.why: Only the list form keeps NAME as one argument that no shell interprets, and `check` and `timeout` make failures loud.

interview.q: When do you write an ops script in Python instead of Bash?
interview.a: When it needs data structures, JSON or HTTP, different handling for different errors, or tests. Bash is good glue for a few commands and short CI steps, but its quoting and error handling get fragile as scripts grow. Python's standard library covers files, JSON, regular expressions, time zones and subprocesses, and behaves the same on macOS and Linux. I keep the Bash habits either way: clear exit codes, messages on stderr and failing loudly.

interview.q: How do you run an external command safely from Python?
interview.a: I use `subprocess.run` with a list of arguments, so no shell parses them and there is no injection risk. I pass `check=True` so a non-zero exit raises `CalledProcessError`, `capture_output=True, text=True` to read its output, and a `timeout` so a hung command cannot hang my script. I avoid `shell=True`, and never use it with outside input. On failure I log the command's stderr and exit with a clear code.

interview.q: Why do scripts have a main() function and `if __name__ == "__main__"`?
interview.a: The guard runs `main` only when the file is executed, not when it is imported. That lets tests import the module and call `main([...])` with their own arguments, then assert on the exit code it returns. Having `main` return an int and calling `sys.exit(main())` keeps the exit-code logic in one place. It also keeps parsing and printing apart from the functions that do the work, which makes them easy to test.

deeper.body:
The summarizer reads a whole file into memory with `read_text()`. For a 238-line practice log that is fine. On a server, access logs can grow to gigabytes, so it is worth knowing what that choice costs.

To find out, we repeated `access.log` 4,200 times: 999,600 lines, 158 MB. Then we parsed it in two ways with the same `parse_access` function:

- `parse_access(read_lines(path))`, which reads everything first, peaked at 384 MB of memory.
- `with path.open() as f: parse_access(f)`, which hands over one line at a time, peaked at 15 MB.

`parse_access` already accepts any iterable of lines, so streaming needed no change inside it. That is a good reason to write parsing functions this way. A file, a list in a test, `sys.stdin` and a decompressed stream all work.

Rotated logs are usually compressed, such as `access.log.2.gz`. The call `gzip.open(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8")` opens one as text, and you can loop over it like any file. Our 158 MB test log compressed to 11 MB, though it repeats itself far more than a real log does. To support pipes as well, accept `-` as the file name and read `sys.stdin`. Then `zcat access.log.*.gz | logsum access -` works the way Unix tools do.

Speed is the other cost. Both runs took 11 to 12 seconds for a million lines. The awk filter `awk '$9 >= 500'` went through the same file in under half a second. A quick profile on 100,000 lines showed where the time goes: the regex took 0.05 seconds, while `datetime.strptime` took 0.79 seconds, about three quarters of the total. Two cheap fixes are open to you:

1. Access logs are written in time order, so you only need to parse the first and the last timestamp, not every one.
2. On a busy server many lines share the same second, so caching parsed values with `functools.lru_cache` avoids parsing the same text twice.

That is the general pattern for Python ops scripts. Write the clear version first, measure on realistic data, and fix the one hot spot the profile shows. The command `uv run python -m cProfile -s cumtime scripts/logsum.py access big.log` prints which functions used the time.

sections.h: The requests library is still the default for scripts
sections.body:
The Day 15 health checker used `urllib.request` from the standard library. That is fine for a status code. Once you need JSON, headers, sessions and retries, use a library. There are two serious choices:

- requests: synchronous, with an API that has barely changed in years, and a mocking library, `responses`, made for it.
- httpx: almost the same API, plus async code and HTTP/2.

For ops scripts, pick requests today. The httpx project has had no stable release since 0.28.1 in December 2024. Its 1.0 has been out only as development releases that change the API, and Pydantic now maintains a fork named httpx2 that keeps the old one. That split will settle. Until it does, a script that runs from cron for three years is better off on the library that does not move. Reach for httpx2 when you really need async or HTTP/2.

Four habits make every call safe:

1. Always pass `timeout=`. Requests has no default, so a server that accepts the connection and never answers hangs your script forever. The value `timeout=(3.05, 10)` waits up to 3.05 seconds to connect, then up to 10 seconds of silence while the answer arrives. It does not limit the whole download. The requests docs suggest a connect value just above a multiple of 3. They call 3 seconds the default TCP retransmission window: the wait before an unanswered packet is sent again.
2. Call `response.raise_for_status()`. A 404 or a 500 is not an exception in requests until you ask for one.
3. Read the body with `response.json()`, after the status check.
4. Use a `requests.Session` for more than one call. It keeps the connection open, so later calls skip the TCP and TLS handshakes (Days 10 and 11), and it sends the same headers every time.

sections.h: Tokens, retries and pages: the GitHub API
sections.body:
The lab's first tool, `gh-runs`, lists a repo's recent GitHub Actions runs and exits 1 when one of them failed. It asks with `GET https://api.github.com/repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs`. Three headers go with every request:

- `Accept: application/vnd.github+json`, the media type GitHub recommends.
- `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10`, the newest API version. Pinning it keeps a later version from changing the JSON under your script. Without the header, GitHub picks one for you; it answered with `2022-11-28` when we left it out.
- `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (whoever bears, or holds, the token gets in), with the token read from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable.

Locally, `export GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)"` borrows the token the gh CLI got on Day 2. In GitHub Actions, the same variable can come from the built-in token (Day 27). The script never prints the token and never takes it as a flag, because flags end up in your shell history and in `ps` output. Without a token you get 60 requests an hour, and with one you get 5,000.

Retry only when asking again can help: a 429 (too many requests), a 502, 503 or 504, or a dropped connection. Never retry a 401 or a 404, because the answer will not change. Retry only idempotent methods (Day 11): a repeated GET is harmless, while a repeated POST may start two deploys. Requests does none of this by default. Under the hood it sends every call through urllib3, a lower-level HTTP library with a `Retry` class. The lab attaches one to the session with `session.mount("https://", ...)`, using `status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504]` and `allowed_methods=["GET"]`. With `backoff_factor=1` it waits 0, then 2, then 4 seconds, and it obeys a `Retry-After` header when the server sends one.

One request returns one page: 30 runs unless you ask for more with `per_page`, and never more than 100. GitHub puts the next page's address in the `Link` header. Requests parses that header into `response.links["next"]["url"]`. The `list_runs` function follows it until there is no next page or it has enough runs.

sections.h: AWS from Python: boto3 sessions, profiles and clients
sections.body:
Boto3 is AWS's SDK (software development kit) for Python. Each method call becomes an HTTPS request to an AWS API, signed with your credentials so AWS knows who is asking. Every script starts from a session, which holds one set of credentials and one region:

- `boto3.Session(profile_name="learn")` uses the `learn` profile from Day 13. Run `aws login --profile learn` first, and boto3 picks up the same sign-in. That needs boto3's `crt` extra, an optional add-on installed as `boto3[crt]`, which the lab's `pyproject.toml` asks for.
- Leave the profile out and boto3 searches the usual places in order: environment variables such as `AWS_PROFILE`, the files in `~/.aws`, and finally a container or instance role (Day 14).
- `session.client("s3")` gives you a client. It has one method per API call, in snake_case, so ListBuckets becomes `list_buckets()`.

Answers are plain dictionaries, shaped like the JSON the CLI printed on Day 13. Errors come in two families:

- `botocore.exceptions.ClientError`: AWS answered with an error. `err.response["Error"]["Code"]` holds a code such as `AccessDenied` or `NoSuchBucket`, and you decide per code.
- `botocore.exceptions.BotoCoreError`: no useful answer at all. No credentials, an unknown profile and an expired sign-in all land here.

Start every AWS script with `sts.get_caller_identity()` and log the account and identity it returns. It is the Python twin of `aws sts get-caller-identity`, it needs no permissions, and it catches "wrong account" before anything else runs.

Use clients, not the older `boto3.resource` interface, which the boto3 docs say will get no new features.

sections.h: Paginators, waiters and a read-only report
sections.body:
Most AWS list calls return one page at a time. For example, `list_objects_v2` returns at most 1,000 keys and a token for the next page. A script that forgets this sees 1,000 objects in a bucket that holds 5,000. A paginator asks for every page for you. The call `ec2.get_paginator("describe_instances").paginate(Filters=[...])` gives an iterator of pages. Then `pages.search("Reservations[].Instances[]")` pulls every instance out of them with JMESPath, the same language as `--query` on Day 13.

When you call `run_instances`, AWS answers while the new instance is still `pending`, so code that uses it at once fails. A waiter polls until a resource reaches a state. The waiter from `ec2.get_waiter("instance_running")` calls DescribeInstances every 15 seconds, up to 40 times, then raises `WaiterError`. The lab uses waiters wherever code creates something and must wait for it: in `seed_moto.py` and in the tests.

The lab's second tool, `aws-report`, puts the pieces together. It only reads, and it needs three permissions: `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, `s3:GetBucketVersioning` and `ec2:DescribeInstances`. It reports two things:

- S3 buckets where versioning is off or suspended. Versioning keeps old copies of objects, so an overwrite or a delete can be undone, which is why Day 13's bucket has it on.
- EC2 instances that still exist and have no `owner` tag, so nobody knows whom to ask before stopping them. Stopped instances count, because their disks still cost money.

A bucket the script may not read becomes a finding, `cannot read versioning (AccessDenied)`, instead of a crash. A report that dies on bucket 3 of 200 tells you nothing about the other 197.

A script that runs at 3 a.m. deserves tests as much as the app it watches. The pytest runner finds files named `test_*.py` and runs every function named `test_*`. When an `assert` fails, it shows the values on both sides. In the lab, `uv run pytest` runs 30 tests in about 8 seconds, offline.

The `main(argv) -> int` shape from Day 15 is what makes this easy: call `main(["access", str(path)])` and assert on the number it returns. Three built-in fixtures do most of the rest. A fixture is something pytest prepares for a test that names it as an argument:

- `tmp_path` is a fresh empty folder for this one test. Write a three-line log into it, with one broken line, instead of depending on real files.
- `monkeypatch` changes things for one test only. `monkeypatch.setenv("LOGSUM_MAX_ERROR_RATE", "50")` and `monkeypatch.delenv("GITHUB_TOKEN")` are undone when the test ends, so no test leaks settings into the next.
- `capsys` captures what the code printed. `out, err = capsys.readouterr()` lets you check that the report went to stdout and the reason went to stderr.

You can write your own fixtures with `@pytest.fixture`, and code after a `yield` inside one runs as cleanup. The file `test_healthcheck.py` uses that to start a real web server on 127.0.0.1 for each test. The server shuts down afterwards, so the 503 and timeout cases are real without leaving the laptop.

What deserves a test in an ops script? The exit codes, the parsing of realistic input including one malformed line, and every error message a tired person will read. Leave argparse and requests alone; their own authors test them.

sections.h: Fake services: responses for HTTP, moto for AWS
sections.body:
Tests that call the real GitHub or AWS are slow and flaky, and they need secrets in CI. Replace the service and keep your code as it is.

`responses` replaces the step where requests hands data to the network, so registered URLs get canned answers instead. Inside a test marked `@responses.activate`, `responses.get(url, json={...}, status=200)` registers one answer. A request to any URL you did not register raises `ConnectionError`, so a test cannot reach the internet by accident. Matchers check what you sent, such as the `Authorization` header. `registries.OrderedRegistry` hands out answers in order, a 502 and then a 200, which proves the retry works. Pass `backoff=0` in that test so it does not sleep.

Moto does the same for AWS. Inside `with mock_aws():`, moto catches each boto3 request just before it would be sent and answers it from an in-memory fake AWS. That fake starts empty for each test. The test creates the buckets and instances it needs, then calls the real function. Two rules from the moto docs:

1. Set fake credentials first, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=testing` and the rest, with `monkeypatch.setenv`. If your shell holds real keys, this makes sure they are never used.
2. Start the mock before you create any client. A client made earlier, for example at import time, is not mocked.

Moto is a model of AWS, not AWS. It does not check IAM permissions unless you ask it to, so a test passes even when the real role would be denied. Run a new check once against a real account before you trust it. The same moto also runs as a server (`moto_server -p 5050`) that boto3 reaches through `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`, the same idea as `--endpoint-url` on Day 13.

sections.h: Ship it: a command, ruff and CI
sections.body:
A folder of scripts becomes a tool when teammates can install it. `pyproject.toml` lists commands under `[project.scripts]`. The line `gh-runs = "python_ops.gh_runs:main"` means: make a command named `gh-runs` that calls `main` in that module. When uv installs the project, with `uv sync` or `uv tool install`, it writes a tiny `gh-runs` launcher into that environment's `bin` folder. It imports the module and runs `sys.exit(main())`, so your exit codes reach the shell. Since uv 0.12, `uv init` creates this kind of project by default. It puts the code under `src/` and packages it with uv's own build backend. Three ways to use the commands:

- `uv run gh-runs ...` inside the project folder.
- `uv tool install --editable .` installs the project into one environment of its own and links both commands into `~/.local/bin` (`uv tool update-shell` puts that folder on your PATH). With `--editable`, your code changes apply without reinstalling.
- `uv tool install git+https://github.com/YOU/python-ops` installs them for a teammate straight from git.

ruff lints and formats in one fast tool. Linting means reading code for likely bugs without running it: `uv run ruff check` does that, and `uv run ruff format` fixes the layout. The lab turns on a few rule groups that suit ops code, each explained in `pyproject.toml`. Three of them earn their place:

- `S113` flags `requests.get(url)` without a timeout. It does not see calls on a `Session`, so the habit still matters.
- `S602` flags `shell=True`, and `PLW1510` flags `subprocess.run` without `check=`.
- `DTZ` flags naive datetimes such as `datetime.now()`.

Last comes CI. The lab's `ci.yml` installs uv with `astral-sh/setup-uv`, runs `uv sync --locked`, then ruff and pytest. `--locked` fails the job when `uv.lock` no longer matches `pyproject.toml`. Each step fails the job through its exit code, just like the scripts themselves. Day 25 builds a full pipeline with caching and a matrix.

code.src:
"""gh-runs: list recent GitHub Actions runs for a repository and fail if any failed.

Examples:
  export GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)"
  uv run gh-runs arunav-bhattacharya/devops-from-zero
  uv run gh-runs YOUR-USER/hello-devops --branch main --limit 50

Exit codes: 0 no failed runs, 1 at least one failed run, 2 could not ask GitHub.
"""

import argparse
import logging
import os
import sys
from datetime import UTC, datetime

import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util import Retry

log = logging.getLogger("gh-runs")

API = "https://api.github.com"
API_VERSION = "2026-03-10"  # pin the API version so a new one cannot change answers under you
TIMEOUT = (3.05, 10)  # seconds to connect, seconds to wait for each part of the answer
FAILED = {"failure", "timed_out", "startup_failure"}


def make_session(token: str | None, retries: int = 3, backoff: float = 1.0) -> requests.Session:
    """A session sends the same headers every time and reuses connections."""
    session = requests.Session()
    session.headers.update(
        {
            "Accept": "application/vnd.github+json",
            "X-GitHub-Api-Version": API_VERSION,
            "User-Agent": "python-ops-gh-runs",
        }
    )
    if token:
        session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
    # Retry GETs on 429 and 5xx, waiting longer each time (and as long as
    # Retry-After asks). Never retry 401 or 404: asking again cannot fix those.
    retry = Retry(
        total=retries,
        backoff_factor=backoff,
        status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
        allowed_methods=["GET"],
        raise_on_status=False,  # hand back the last answer, so we can explain it
    )
    session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))
    return session


def list_runs(
    session: requests.Session,
    repo: str,
    limit: int,
    branch: str | None = None,
    per_page: int = 100,
) -> list[dict]:
    """Return up to `limit` runs, newest first, following GitHub's pages."""
    url = f"{API}/repos/{repo}/actions/runs"
    params: dict | None = {"per_page": min(limit, per_page)}
    if branch:
        params["branch"] = branch
    runs: list[dict] = []
    while url and len(runs) < limit:
        response = session.get(url, params=params, timeout=TIMEOUT)
        response.raise_for_status()
        runs.extend(response.json()["workflow_runs"])
        # The Link header holds the URL of the next page, query string included.
        url = response.links.get("next", {}).get("url")
        params = None
    return runs[:limit]


def explain(err: requests.HTTPError) -> str:
    """Turn an HTTP error into a sentence a person can act on."""
    response = err.response
    status = response.status_code
    if status == 401:
        return "GitHub says 401: the token is wrong or expired. Try: gh auth status"
    if status in (403, 429) and response.headers.get("x-ratelimit-remaining") == "0":
        reset = int(response.headers.get("x-ratelimit-reset", "0"))
        when = datetime.fromtimestamp(reset, tz=UTC).strftime("%H:%M UTC")
        return f"rate limit used up; it resets at {when}. A token raises the limit."
    if status == 404:
        return "GitHub says 404: no such repo, or your token cannot see it."
    return f"GitHub answered {status}: {response.text[:200]}"


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="gh-runs", description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("repo", help="OWNER/NAME, for example octocat/hello-world")
    parser.add_argument("--branch", help="only runs for this branch")
    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=20, help="how many runs (default 20)")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--per-page", type=int, default=100, help="runs per request (default and maximum 100)"
    )
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", help="log every HTTP request")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.WARNING,
        format="%(name)s: %(message)s",
        stream=sys.stderr,
        force=True,
    )

    if args.repo.count("/") != 1:
        parser.error("repo must look like OWNER/NAME")  # prints usage and exits with 2
    token = os.environ.get("GITHUB_TOKEN")
    if not token:
        log.warning("GITHUB_TOKEN is not set: public repos only, 60 requests an hour")

    try:
        session = make_session(token)
        runs = list_runs(session, args.repo, args.limit, args.branch, args.per_page)
    except requests.HTTPError as err:
        log.error("%s", explain(err))
        return 2
    except requests.RequestException as err:
        # DNS failure, refused connection, timeout, too many retries
        log.error("could not reach GitHub: %s", err)
        return 2

    failed = [run for run in runs if run["conclusion"] in FAILED]
    for run in runs:
        result = run["conclusion"] or run["status"]  # conclusion is null while a run is going
        created = run["created_at"].replace("T", " ").removesuffix("Z")
        branch = run["head_branch"]
        print(f"#{run['run_number']:<5} {result:<10} {branch:<20} {created}  {run['name']}")
    print(f"{len(runs)} runs, {len(failed)} failed")
    for run in failed:
        log.error("failed: %s #%s %s", run["name"], run["run_number"], run["html_url"])
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

"""aws-report: find S3 buckets without versioning and EC2 instances without an owner tag.

Examples:
  aws login --profile learn          # the sign-in from Day 13
  uv run aws-report --profile learn --region us-east-1
  AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:5050 uv run aws-report   # a local moto server

The report only reads: it calls List, Get and Describe APIs and changes nothing.
Exit codes: 0 nothing found, 1 findings, 2 could not ask AWS.
"""

import argparse
import json
import logging
import sys

import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import BotoCoreError, ClientError

log = logging.getLogger("aws-report")

# Instances in these states still exist (and stopped ones can still cost money for disks).
LIVE_STATES = ["pending", "running", "stopping", "stopped"]


def buckets_without_versioning(s3) -> list[dict]:
    findings = []
    # list_buckets returns pages too; a paginator asks for every page for you.
    for page in s3.get_paginator("list_buckets").paginate():
        for bucket in page.get("Buckets", []):
            name = bucket["Name"]
            try:
                answer = s3.get_bucket_versioning(Bucket=name)
            except ClientError as err:
                # One bucket we may not read should not hide the rest of the report.
                code = err.response["Error"]["Code"]
                findings.append({"bucket": name, "problem": f"cannot read versioning ({code})"})
                continue
            # "Enabled", "Suspended", or no Status at all (never turned on).
            status = answer.get("Status", "Disabled")
            if status != "Enabled":
                findings.append({"bucket": name, "problem": f"versioning {status.lower()}"})
    return findings


def instances_without_owner(ec2, tag_key: str = "owner") -> list[dict]:
    findings = []
    pages = ec2.get_paginator("describe_instances").paginate(
        Filters=[{"Name": "instance-state-name", "Values": LIVE_STATES}]
    )
    # search() runs a JMESPath expression (as in --query on Day 13) over every page.
    for instance in pages.search("Reservations[].Instances[]"):
        tags = {t["Key"].lower(): t["Value"] for t in instance.get("Tags", [])}
        if not tags.get(tag_key.lower()):
            findings.append(
                {
                    "instance": instance["InstanceId"],
                    "state": instance["State"]["Name"],
                    "name": tags.get("name", "-"),
                    "problem": f"no {tag_key} tag",
                }
            )
    return findings


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="aws-report", description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--profile", help="profile from ~/.aws/config (default: AWS_PROFILE)")
    parser.add_argument("--region", help="region for EC2 (default: from the profile)")
    parser.add_argument("--owner-tag", default="owner", help="tag every instance needs")
    parser.add_argument("--format", choices=["text", "json"], default="text")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    # Our own messages at INFO; other libraries (botocore) only from WARNING up.
    logging.basicConfig(format="%(name)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stderr, force=True)
    log.setLevel(logging.INFO)

    try:
        # A session holds one set of credentials and one region; clients come from it.
        session = boto3.Session(profile_name=args.profile, region_name=args.region)
        who = session.client("sts").get_caller_identity()
        log.info("account %s, region %s, as %s", who["Account"], session.region_name, who["Arn"])
        buckets = buckets_without_versioning(session.client("s3"))
        instances = instances_without_owner(session.client("ec2"), args.owner_tag)
    except ClientError as err:
        error = err.response["Error"]
        log.error("AWS said %s: %s", error["Code"], error["Message"])
        return 2
    except BotoCoreError as err:
        # No credentials, an unknown profile, an expired sign-in, no region, no network
        log.error("%s", err)
        return 2

    if args.format == "json":
        print(json.dumps({"buckets": buckets, "instances": instances}, indent=2))
    else:
        print(f"S3 buckets without versioning: {len(buckets)}")
        for f in buckets:
            print(f"  {f['bucket']:<40} {f['problem']}")
        print(f"EC2 instances missing the {args.owner_tag} tag: {len(instances)}")
        for f in instances:
            print(f"  {f['instance']:<22} {f['state']:<9} {f['name']}")
    return 1 if buckets or instances else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

"""Tests for aws-report. moto plays AWS inside this process: nothing leaves your laptop."""

import boto3
import pytest
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
from moto import mock_aws

from python_ops import aws_report

REGION = "eu-central-1"


@pytest.fixture
def aws(monkeypatch):
    """Fake credentials first, then moto. Real keys in your shell can never be used."""
    for name in ("AWS_PROFILE", "AWS_ENDPOINT_URL", "AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"):
        monkeypatch.delenv(name, raising=False)
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "testing")
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "testing")
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION", REGION)
    with mock_aws():
        yield


def make_bucket(s3, name, versioning=None):
    s3.create_bucket(Bucket=name, CreateBucketConfiguration={"LocationConstraint": REGION})
    if versioning:
        s3.put_bucket_versioning(Bucket=name, VersioningConfiguration={"Status": versioning})


def make_instance(ec2, tags):
    image = ec2.describe_images(Owners=["amazon"])["Images"][0]["ImageId"]
    answer = ec2.run_instances(
        ImageId=image,
        InstanceType="t4g.micro",
        MinCount=1,
        MaxCount=1,
        TagSpecifications=[
            {"ResourceType": "instance", "Tags": [{"Key": k, "Value": v} for k, v in tags.items()]}
        ],
    )
    instance_id = answer["Instances"][0]["InstanceId"]
    # The waiter polls describe_instances until the state is "running".
    ec2.get_waiter("instance_running").wait(InstanceIds=[instance_id])
    return instance_id


def test_buckets_without_versioning(aws):
    s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=REGION)
    make_bucket(s3, "never-versioned")
    make_bucket(s3, "versioned", versioning="Enabled")
    make_bucket(s3, "paused", versioning="Suspended")
    findings = aws_report.buckets_without_versioning(s3)
    assert findings == [
        {"bucket": "never-versioned", "problem": "versioning disabled"},
        {"bucket": "paused", "problem": "versioning suspended"},
    ]


def test_instances_without_owner(aws):
    ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name=REGION)
    make_instance(ec2, {"Name": "web-1", "owner": "ana"})
    lost = make_instance(ec2, {"Name": "test-box"})
    shouting = make_instance(ec2, {"Name": "db-1", "Owner": "li"})  # tag keys differ in case
    findings = aws_report.instances_without_owner(ec2)
    assert [f["instance"] for f in findings] == [lost]
    assert shouting not in [f["instance"] for f in findings]


def test_terminated_instances_are_ignored(aws):
    ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name=REGION)
    gone = make_instance(ec2, {"Name": "old"})
    ec2.terminate_instances(InstanceIds=[gone])
    ec2.get_waiter("instance_terminated").wait(InstanceIds=[gone])
    assert aws_report.instances_without_owner(ec2) == []


def test_unreadable_bucket_is_reported_not_fatal(aws, monkeypatch):
    s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=REGION)
    make_bucket(s3, "locked")

    def access_denied(**kwargs):
        raise ClientError(
            {"Error": {"Code": "AccessDenied", "Message": "Access Denied"}}, "GetBucketVersioning"
        )

    monkeypatch.setattr(s3, "get_bucket_versioning", access_denied)
    findings = aws_report.buckets_without_versioning(s3)
    assert findings == [{"bucket": "locked", "problem": "cannot read versioning (AccessDenied)"}]


def test_main_exit_codes_and_output(aws, capsys):
    assert aws_report.main(["--region", REGION]) == 0  # an empty account is clean
    make_bucket(boto3.client("s3", region_name=REGION), "shop-logs")
    assert aws_report.main(["--region", REGION]) == 1
    out, err = capsys.readouterr()
    assert "S3 buckets without versioning: 1" in out
    assert "account 123456789012" in err  # moto's pretend account number


def test_no_credentials_exits_2(monkeypatch, tmp_path, capsys):
    for name in ("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "AWS_SESSION_TOKEN", "AWS_PROFILE"):
        monkeypatch.delenv(name, raising=False)
    # Point boto3 at empty config files, and stop it from asking EC2's metadata service.
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_CONFIG_FILE", str(tmp_path / "config"))
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE", str(tmp_path / "credentials"))
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED", "true")
    assert aws_report.main(["--region", REGION]) == 2
    assert "Unable to locate credentials" in capsys.readouterr().err

"""seed_moto.py: create a few fake resources in a local moto server for aws-report.

Start the server first, in another terminal:
  uvx --from "moto[server]" moto_server -p 5050
Then:
  export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:5050 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=testing \
         AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=testing AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=eu-central-1
  uv run scripts/seed_moto.py

It refuses to run unless AWS_ENDPOINT_URL points at your own machine, so it can
never create anything in a real AWS account.
"""

import os
import sys
from urllib.parse import urlparse

import boto3

REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION", "eu-central-1")


def main() -> int:
    endpoint = os.environ.get("AWS_ENDPOINT_URL", "")
    if urlparse(endpoint).hostname not in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1"):
        print("seed_moto: set AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:5050 first", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=REGION)
    where = {"LocationConstraint": REGION}
    for name in ("shop-invoices", "shop-tmp-exports", "shop-backups"):
        s3.create_bucket(Bucket=name, CreateBucketConfiguration=where)
        # A waiter asks again and again until the bucket exists, or gives up.
        s3.get_waiter("bucket_exists").wait(Bucket=name)
    s3.put_bucket_versioning(Bucket="shop-backups", VersioningConfiguration={"Status": "Enabled"})

    ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name=REGION)
    image = ec2.describe_images(Owners=["amazon"])["Images"][0]["ImageId"]
    tagged = ec2.run_instances(
        ImageId=image,
        InstanceType="t4g.micro",
        MinCount=1,
        MaxCount=1,
        TagSpecifications=[
            {
                "ResourceType": "instance",
                "Tags": [{"Key": "Name", "Value": "web-1"}, {"Key": "owner", "Value": "ana"}],
            }
        ],
    )
    untagged = ec2.run_instances(
        ImageId=image,
        InstanceType="t4g.micro",
        MinCount=1,
        MaxCount=1,
        TagSpecifications=[
            {"ResourceType": "instance", "Tags": [{"Key": "Name", "Value": "test-box"}]}
        ],
    )
    ids = [r["Instances"][0]["InstanceId"] for r in (tagged, untagged)]
    ec2.get_waiter("instance_running").wait(InstanceIds=ids)
    print(f"seed_moto: 3 buckets and 2 running instances ({', '.join(ids)}) in {REGION}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# ci.yml: lint and test python-ops on every push to main and every pull request.
# GitHub only reads .github/ at the root of a repository, so this runs once
# python-ops is its own repo (Day 16), not inside the course repo.
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # setup-uv publishes no short "v10" tag, so name the full version.
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
        with:
          enable-cache: true
      # --locked fails if uv.lock no longer matches pyproject.toml.
      # uv reads .python-version and installs that Python.
      - name: Install Python and the locked dependencies
        run: uv sync --locked
      - name: Lint and format check
        run: uv run ruff check && uv run ruff format --check
      - name: Tests
        run: uv run pytest

lessons.mistake: Creating a boto3 client at the top of a module, `s3 = boto3.client("s3")`, and then starting moto inside the test. The client already exists when the mock starts, so moto may not intercept it, and the test can reach real AWS with whatever credentials your shell had. Create clients inside functions, or pass them in, and start `mock_aws()` with fake credentials before any client is made.
lessons.real_world: Untagged instances are the ones nobody dares to stop, and buckets without versioning are the ones nobody can restore. Platform teams run a read-only report like `aws-report` on a schedule in every account. It assumes a role that can only list and describe, and it posts the findings to the owning team's channel. The report has moto tests in CI, so a change to it cannot break the Monday run.

task.title: Teach aws-report to find SSH open to the world
steps: In terminal 1, start a fake AWS: `uvx --from "moto[server]" moto_server -p 5050`.

In terminal 2, in `~/code/python-ops`, export `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:5050`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=testing`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=testing` and `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=eu-central-1`. Then run `uv run scripts/seed_moto.py` and `uv run aws-report`.

Create a security group that allows port 22 from `0.0.0.0/0` in moto with the AWS CLI from Day 13: `aws ec2 create-security-group` and `aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress`, with the same endpoint.
Add a function `ssh_open_to_world(ec2)` to `aws_report.py`. It goes through every security group with a paginator and reports groups whose rules allow port 22 from `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0`.
Call it from `main`, print the findings in text and JSON, and include them in the exit code.
Write a moto test with three groups: SSH from `0.0.0.0/0`, SSH from `10.0.0.0/8` and HTTPS from `0.0.0.0/0`. Only the first may be reported.
Run `uv run pytest` and `uv run ruff check`, and fix anything they report.
Run `uv run aws-report` against the moto server again and check that your group appears and the exit code is 1.
Optional, with a real account: run `aws login --profile learn`, then `uv run aws-report --profile learn`. It only reads, so it costs nothing.
hints: `describe_security_groups` has a paginator; each group has `IpPermissions`, and each permission has `FromPort`, `ToPort`, `IpRanges` and `Ipv6Ranges`.
`IpProtocol` of `"-1"` means all traffic, and then there is no `FromPort`; read the ports with `.get()`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how you make a script that calls an API safe to run in CI, and how you test it without the network. Mention timeouts, retries and mocks.
explain_back.answer: Every call gets a timeout, so a silent server cannot hang the job. Retries go only to errors that may pass, such as 429 and 5xx, only for idempotent methods, with growing waits, and never for 401 or 404. Errors become one clear line on stderr and a non-zero exit code, and the token comes from an environment variable. In tests, responses answers in place of the HTTP API and moto in place of AWS, so pytest can check retries, failures and exit codes offline.

recap: Use requests for scripts, and always pass a timeout and call raise_for_status().
Retry 429 and 5xx with backoff on idempotent methods only; never retry 401 or 404.
Follow the Link header or a boto3 paginator, or you only see the first page.
A boto3 session holds one profile and region; catch ClientError and BotoCoreError separately.
Test with tmp_path, monkeypatch and capsys; fake HTTP with responses and AWS with moto.
[project.scripts] plus `uv tool install` turns scripts into commands; ruff and CI keep them honest.

check.q: A cleanup script lists objects with `s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket=b)` and deletes the old ones. The bucket holds 4,000 objects. What happens?
options: It sees every object, since boto3 pages automatically
It raises an error asking for a paginator
It only sees the first 1,000 objects
It sees nothing until versioning is enabled
check.why: A single call returns at most 1,000 keys; use `get_paginator("list_objects_v2")` to get every page.

check.q: A script sends `POST /deployments` through a session whose urllib3 `Retry` lists 502 in `status_forcelist` but keeps the default allowed methods. The API answers 502. What happens?
options: It returns the 502, since POST is not retried by default
It retries the POST three times with backoff
It turns the POST into a GET and retries
It retries once, and only after waiting 60 seconds
check.why: urllib3 retries only idempotent methods by default, because repeating a POST could create two deployments.

check.q: A test marked `@responses.activate` registers only `/actions/runs`, but the code also calls `/rate_limit`. What happens in the test?
options: The call goes to the real api.github.com
requests returns an empty 200 answer
The test is skipped with a warning
requests raises ConnectionError for the unregistered URL
check.why: responses refuses every URL you did not register, so a test can never reach the network by accident.

interview.q: How do you make HTTP calls from a script reliable?
interview.a: Every call has a timeout, because requests waits forever by default. I use a Session so headers and connections are reused, and I mount a retry policy that retries 429 and 5xx answers with exponential backoff and honours Retry-After. Only idempotent methods are retried, and 401 or 404 never are. After the call I check the status with raise_for_status, and I turn errors into a clear message and a non-zero exit code.

interview.q: How do you test code that calls AWS?
interview.a: For unit tests I use moto's mock_aws, which fakes AWS in memory. I set fake credentials first, so real ones can never be used. Each test creates the resources it needs and then calls the real function, with every client created after the mock starts. Moto does not check IAM by default, so I also run new checks once against a sandbox account with a least-privilege role. For error paths that are hard to fake, I raise a ClientError myself with monkeypatch or use botocore's Stubber.

interview.q: What are boto3 paginators and waiters for?
interview.a: Many AWS list calls return one page of results plus a token, so code that makes one call silently misses data. A paginator follows the tokens for you, and its search method can pull items out of every page with JMESPath. A waiter polls a describe call until a resource reaches a state, such as an instance running. It waits a fixed delay between tries and gives up after a maximum number of attempts. Both replace hand-written loops that are easy to get wrong.

deeper.body:
Kubernetes has an official Python client too, the `kubernetes` package. Part 10 teaches clusters with kubectl; this is what the same questions look like from Python, once you have a cluster.

The client reads the same kubeconfig as kubectl:

1. `config.load_kube_config()` loads `~/.kube/config` and its current context, exactly like kubectl on your laptop.
2. `v1 = client.CoreV1Api()` gives an API object for the core resources: pods, services, namespaces.
3. `v1.list_pod_for_all_namespaces(watch=False)` returns objects with attributes, so `pod.metadata.name` and `pod.status.phase` work without any JSON parsing.

Inside a pod, use `config.load_incluster_config()` instead. It reads the token and the CA certificate that Kubernetes mounts for the pod's service account, so no kubeconfig file is needed. What the script may do is then decided by RBAC rules for that service account (Day 64). A read-only report needs only `get` and `list` on the resources it reads.

A report in the style of today's tools would list pods that are not Ready: for each pod, look at `pod.status.conditions` for the condition of type `Ready` with status `False`. Then print a table, return 1 when the list is not empty, and test it with a fake object instead of a cluster. Because the client returns objects, a test can build a few with `client.V1Pod(...)` and pass them to your function, with no network at all.

The client also supports watching. `watch.Watch().stream(v1.list_namespace, _request_timeout=60)` yields an event every time a namespace is added, changed or deleted. Set a timeout here too, for the same reason as with requests.

When should you use the client rather than `subprocess.run(["kubectl", "get", "pods", "-o", "json"], ...)` plus `json.loads`? The kubectl route is fine for a quick script on your laptop, and its output matches what you see in the terminal. The client wins for anything that runs inside the cluster, needs watches, or should not depend on a kubectl binary being installed. The package's major version follows Kubernetes releases, and its README has a compatibility table, so pick the version that matches your cluster, as you did with kubectl itself.

Start from the examples in the [Kubernetes Python client README](https://github.com/kubernetes-client/python). They run against the kind cluster you build in Part 10.

quiz.q: A teammate's 300-line Bash script parses JSON with five jq calls and keeps a list of hosts with settings. What is the strongest reason to rewrite it in Python?
options: Python scripts always run faster than Bash scripts do
Its data and JSON are easier to handle and test in Python
Bash scripts cannot run in GitHub Actions workflows
Python needs no installation on a Mac or on Linux
quiz.why: Data structures, JSON and tests are where Bash gets fragile and Python is strong; speed is not the reason.

quiz.q: You run `uv run scripts/report.py` inside a project, and the script starts with a `# /// script` block. Which packages does it get?
options: The project's dependencies plus the block's
Only the project's dependencies from uv.lock
Only the packages listed in the script's block
None, until you activate .venv
quiz.why: A script with inline metadata ignores the project and runs in its own environment built from its block.

quiz.q: A summarizer prints a JSON report and also prints progress lines with `print()`. `| jq` fails. What is the right fix?
options: Send the progress lines to stderr with logging
Add the `--raw-output` flag to the jq command
Print the whole JSON report on a single line
Remove the progress lines and the exit code
quiz.why: stdout must hold only the data; messages for people belong on stderr, where jq never sees them.

quiz.q: Which exit-code contract lets CI tell 'the check failed' apart from 'the script could not run'?
options: 0 on success, and 1 for every kind of failure
0 all good, 1 the check found a problem, 2 the script could not do its job
Always exit 0 and print FAILED when something is wrong
Exit with the number of problems found, up to 1000
quiz.why: Separate codes let a caller react differently to a real finding and to a broken run; codes also stop at 255.

quiz.q: GitHub answers your script with 403 and `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0`. What should the script do?
options: Retry straight away, up to three more times
Switch the request to the newest API version
Treat it as a bad token and print the token
Stop and report when x-ratelimit-reset says it resets
quiz.why: Retrying before the reset time cannot succeed; say when it resets and exit non-zero.

quiz.q: A test sets fake AWS keys with monkeypatch and starts `mock_aws()`, but the module under test created `s3 = boto3.client("s3")` at import time. What is the risk?
options: moto runs slower than usual
pytest refuses to import the module
The fake keys leak into other tests
The client may not be mocked and can call real AWS
quiz.why: moto must be active before a client is created; an earlier client may bypass the mock.

quiz.q: Which ruff rule in the lab flags `requests.get(url)` with no timeout, and what does it miss?
options: S113; it does not see calls made on a requests Session
DTZ005; it misses POST requests
PLW1510; it misses calls inside tests
S602; it misses calls with headers
quiz.why: S113 checks module-level requests calls, so `session.get` without a timeout still needs your own habit.

quiz.q: Why does the lab's CI run `uv sync --locked` instead of `uv sync`?
options: It installs the packages faster from the cache
It skips the dev group so CI images stay small
It fails when uv.lock no longer matches pyproject.toml
It upgrades every package to the newest version
quiz.why: --locked turns a stale lock file into a red build instead of quietly resolving new versions in CI.

quiz.q: A Bash script with `set -euo pipefail` runs `grep -q FATAL app.log` and the log has no FATAL lines. What happens?
options: The script carries on, because grep printed nothing
grep prints an error and the script carries on
The script stops, because grep exits 1 when nothing matches
pipefail turns the result into exit code 0
quiz.why: grep exits 1 on no match, and `-e` stops the script; write `|| true` when no match is fine. Python's check=True behaves the same way.

quiz.q: Your retry policy covers 503 answers. Which request is safe to retry automatically?
options: POST /payments without an idempotency key
GET /api/orders/1001
POST /deployments
PATCH /accounts/7 that adds 10 to a balance
quiz.why: GET is idempotent, so repeating it changes nothing; the others can charge, deploy or add twice (Day 11).
